stars.name: HL Tauri
stars.description: Young star surrounded by an ALMA-resolved planet-forming disc.

position.credit: ALMA Partnership et al. (2015), ApJL 808, L3, Table 1 (Band 6 continuum peak, ICRS/J2000 at epoch 2014.83) and Section 3.1.1 (proper motion, mas/yr, RA including cos Dec)

distance.source: Pinte et al. (2016), Section 1; the adopted Taurus distance used by both this model and the ALMA ring radii

temperature.source: Pinte et al. (2016), Section 3.1: adopted stellar effective temperature, a model input

radius.source: Model radius derived from Pinte et al. (2016), Section 3.1: L = 11 solar luminosities and T = 4000 K; R/Rsun = sqrt(11) (5772/4000)^2, using the IAU nominal solar temperature. No resolved stellar radius is measured here

mass.source: Pinte et al. (2016), Sections 3.1 and 5: central mass inferred from the CO and HCO+ gas kinematics

radialVelocity.source: No heliocentric stellar radial velocity is supplied by this reconstruction. Zero is assumed for display propagation; the paper gives gas velocities in the LSR frame, which are not substituted for it

limb.none: The star is an unresolved sphere using the published disc model’s adopted stellar parameters. No resolved photosphere or applicable measured limb law is claimed.

color.reason: ALMA Partnership et al. (2015), Section 1, describes a heavily obscured star with no directly detected optical photosphere. Its reference sphere uses the 4000 K stellar model of Pinte et al. (2016), rather than treating scattered optical light as a photospheric spectrum.

text.card: A young star surrounded by a disc of bright dust rings and dark gaps.
text.introduction: ALMA resolves HL Tauri’s planet-forming disc into nested rings. The disc’s depth is modeled; the star is an unresolved model sphere.
text.locator: Pinte et al. (2016), Sections 1 and 3.1; ALMA Partnership et al. (2015), Sections 1 and 3.1.3

notes: The disc’s millimeter emission is observed; its third dimension is a thin-disc reconstruction.
The stellar temperature and radius are model inputs, not a resolved image of the photosphere.
No planets are placed in the gaps: the image does not measure their positions.
